//1: Drop this file into one of:
//4: or pass it explicitly via:  mcplense scan @ec-foo --profiles ./targets.json
//7: Many enterprise MCPs gate access on custom headers (organization id, project id,
//8: repository id, ...). The `targets` block binds an exact URL to a fixed set of
//9: headers; the CLI can reference these targets positionally via @<name> instead of
//13: The `targetPatterns` block applies headers to every URL matching a glob. Useful
//14: when an entire host or path tree shares a default header set. Patterns are the
//15: LEAST-specific layer of the resolver: named target entries override pattern
//16: entries, and CLI --header flags override both. Per-header-key last-write-wins.
//19: `scope: "All"` (default) extends the headers to BOTH the MCP session AND the
//20: same-origin probes the scanner runs (transport probe, CORS preflight, ...).
//21: `scope: "Session"` keeps the probes bare so you can observe how an UN-
//22: authenticated request looks. Cross-origin probes (e.g. the authorization-
//23: server metadata fetch on login.microsoftonline.com) NEVER get these headers,
//24: regardless of scope, because mixing them across origins would be a leak.
//27: Header values run through the standard env-expander: 'env:VAR' (whole), '${VAR}'

targets.name: ec-bar
targets.//: Some servers gate everything behind these headers. With scope=All (the default),
targets.//1: the transport probe / CORS preflight / authenticated-headers probe all carry the
targets.//2: headers too, so the scan reaches the same surface the live MCP client would.

targets.name: ec-probe-bare
targets.//: scope=Session keeps the unauthenticated probes header-free so you can observe
targets.//1: the bare server-response surface independently of the per-target headers.
